The defendant, 31, a retail store manager, is charged with assault after a fight outside a sports bar at about 11:40 p.m. The complainant suffered a broken nose and needed six stitches above the left eye.

A security camera above the bar entrance shows the defendant striking the complainant in the face. The complainant then steps back with both hands lowered, and about two seconds later the defendant steps forward and strikes a second time. The camera does not cover the two or three seconds before the first punch, because both people stepped partly out of frame. The bouncer testified that the two had argued inside over a spilled drink and that the defendant said "this isn't over" on the way out.

The defendant testified that the complainant followed the defendant outside, shouted threats, and shoved the defendant hard against a parked car, that the defendant punched to get free, and that the defendant still felt threatened when the defendant threw the second punch. Responding officers noted no marks on the defendant and no damage to the parked car. The complainant testified to being punched without warning while walking to a car.

The defendant, 26, a bank loan officer, is charged with assault for a beating at a bus stop at around 10:15 p.m. The complainant suffered a fractured wrist and bruised ribs and could not describe the attacker, who wore a dark jacket with the hood up. The attacker took the complainant's phone.

A food truck worker about 15 meters away watched the attack under a streetlight. Four days later, the worker picked the defendant out of a six-photo lineup and told the detective, "I'm pretty sure, maybe 80 percent." The next morning, a building manager found the complainant's phone case, with the complainant's ID card still inside, in a trash bin behind the apartment building where the defendant lives. The building has 48 units, and the bus stop is about a 12-minute walk away.

The defendant testified that the defendant was at home all evening. Phone records show no activity on the defendant's phone between 9:40 p.m. and 10:45 p.m. The defendant's roommate testified that the defendant was home but admitted to falling asleep at around 10:00 p.m.

The defendant, 38, a city bus driver, is charged with assault after a confrontation in a convenience store parking lot. The complainant suffered a concussion and a cut on the scalp that required staples.

The defendant admits pushing the complainant, who fell and hit the curb. The defendant testified that the two had a short argument about a parking space, and that the complainant then grabbed a glass bottle from a trash bin and swung it at the defendant's head. The defendant said the defendant pushed the complainant away to avoid being hit.

No bottle was recovered, and officers found no broken glass near the spot where the complainant fell. The store clerk testified to glancing at the lot in the reflection of the front window and seeing the complainant "already turning toward their car" when the defendant pushed with both hands. The clerk admitted that the glimpse lasted about a second and that posters covered part of the window. The complainant denied picking up anything and said the defendant came at them from behind.

The defendant called 911 right after the fall and stayed at the scene until police arrived.

The defendant, 29, a line cook, is charged with assault after a fight in the kitchen of the restaurant where the defendant worked. The complainant, a coworker, suffered a deep bruise on the forearm and a sprained shoulder.

The complainant testified that the defendant became angry over an order mix-up and struck them twice with a metal ladle. A dishwasher, who is a close friend of the complainant, supported that version. A second cook, who carpools with the defendant, testified that the complainant grabbed the defendant's collar first and that the defendant raised the ladle only to block.

The emergency physician testified that the forearm bruise could come either from a blow or from a defensive block against a held object. The kitchen camera was broken that week.

Text messages show that the defendant wrote to a friend that night: "I lost it at work, I really messed up." The defendant testified that the message referred to yelling during the argument, not to hitting anyone.

The defendant, 34, an insurance claims adjuster, is charged with assault after a neighbor was found injured in the shared driveway of a duplex at about 7:00 p.m. The complainant suffered a fractured cheekbone and could not identify the attacker, saying they were struck from behind.

Material under the complainant's fingernails contained the defendant's DNA. The two had a long-running dispute about parking, and a third neighbor recorded a phone video at about 1:00 p.m. that day showing the two pushing and grabbing each other for about ten seconds before separating.

The defendant testified that the defendant left for a client inspection at 3:00 p.m. and returned after 8:00 p.m. The client confirmed that the defendant left the inspection site at about 6:15 p.m.; the drive back takes about 35 minutes. A neighbor across the street testified to seeing the defendant's car parked in the driveway "around seven, maybe a little before or after," while taking out the trash, and could not be more precise. A wooden board with traces of the complainant's blood was found by the driveway, without usable fingerprints.

The defendant, 27, a hotel front desk clerk, is charged with assault after punching a stranger at a late-night food stand. The complainant lost a tooth and suffered a cut lip.

The defendant admits throwing one punch. The defendant testified that the complainant was standing very close to the defendant's friend, yelling, and had pulled back a fist, and that the defendant struck first to stop what the defendant believed was an imminent attack on the friend. The friend testified to the same account.

The complainant testified to complaining about the friend cutting in line and said there was no raised fist. The vendor testified that the complainant was "loud and in the friend's face" but could not see the complainant's hands because of the counter. The next morning, the friend texted the defendant: "they were just yelling, you didn't need to swing." At trial, the friend said the message was about a different argument earlier that night, which no one else saw.

A phone video taken by a customer begins just after the punch and shows the complainant on the ground and the defendant stepping back.

The defendant, 42, a real estate agent, is charged with assault after a former business partner was attacked in a parking garage at 9:20 p.m. The complainant suffered a broken arm.

The complainant testified to recognizing the defendant clearly in the garage lights, from about two meters away, and to being hit with a metal pipe. The two had run a small property management business together until it closed eight months earlier, and the complainant was suing the defendant over unpaid debts. The garage cameras were not recording that night due to a power issue. No pipe was recovered.

The day before the attack, the defendant sent the complainant a text message: "You'll regret this lawsuit." The defendant testified that the defendant meant the legal costs the complainant would face, not violence.

A parking attendant saw a person in a gray rain jacket leave the garage on foot right after the attack but did not see the face. The defendant owns a gray rain jacket. The defendant testified that the defendant was at home alone watching television. The defendant's phone shows no activity between 8:00 p.m. and 10:30 p.m., and the defendant's home is about 20 minutes from the garage.

The defendant, 24, a college student who works part-time at a grocery store, is charged with assault after a house party. The complainant was found in the backyard with bruises on the face and a cracked rib.

At the hospital, the complainant told officers that "the person in the green shirt" pushed them down the back steps and kicked them. The defendant was wearing a green shirt that night. Two other guests also wore green, according to party photos. At trial, the complainant said the defendant punched them before the fall, a detail not in the first statement. The complainant's blood alcohol level was 0.19.

Another guest testified to seeing the defendant and the complainant arguing on the porch, next to the back steps, shortly before the complainant was found. The defendant admits the argument, about a borrowed speaker, but says the defendant went back inside and left soon after. A ride-share receipt shows the defendant requested a ride three minutes after the time a guest estimated the fall happened, and was picked up at the front door. The guest who found the complainant said the estimate could be off by ten minutes either way.

The defendant, 36, a hospital lab technician, is charged with assault after a stranger was beaten on a jogging trail early in the morning. The complainant suffered a fractured jaw and described the attacker only as a person in a gray sweatshirt.

The defendant was stopped near the trail about an hour later, wearing a gray sweatshirt. In a recorded police interview that lasted four hours, the defendant eventually said, "Fine, maybe I hit someone, I don't remember." Medical records show the defendant had taken a prescribed sedative the night before. The defendant had waived the right to a lawyer in writing.

In the interview, the defendant said the fight happened "by the bridge," but the attack took place about 800 meters from the bridge. A trail camera captured a person in a gray sweatshirt running away from the area, but the image is too blurry to show the face.

The defendant testified that the defendant walks the trail daily after night shifts and that the defendant only agreed with the detectives so the interview would end.

The defendant, 45, a property manager, is charged with assault after a confrontation near an ATM. The complainant suffered two broken ribs and facial bruises.

The defendant testified that the complainant approached the defendant at the ATM, demanded money, and grabbed the defendant's wallet, and that the defendant wrestled the complainant to the ground and held them there until the threat ended. The complainant denies demanding anything and testified to asking the defendant only for directions.

A bank camera shows the two struggling. The footage shows the defendant on top of the complainant, delivering at least three blows while the complainant appears to be covering their head. The camera has no audio. The defendant's wallet was found on the ground about a meter away. A passerby who called 911 testified to hearing someone yell "give it back" but could not say who yelled it.

The defendant testified that the defendant could not tell whether the complainant had stopped resisting and that the defendant feared the complainant had a weapon. No weapon was found.

The defendant, 33, an insurance agent, is charged with retail theft after leaving a home improvement store with merchandise worth $612 that had not been paid for.

The defendant used a self-checkout station to buy 14 items. The receipt shows payment for 11 items totaling $96. The three unpaid items were a cordless drill, a battery pack, and a set of drill bits, the most expensive items in the cart. A loss prevention officer watched the transaction on camera and stopped the defendant past the exit doors.

The store's maintenance log shows that this station had 23 recorded scanning errors in the previous month, including items that beeped but did not register. The video shows the defendant passing the drill over the scanner, but the screen is not visible. The officer testified that the defendant "did not look at the screen once."

The defendant testified that the defendant did not notice the missing items and offered to pay when stopped.

The defendant, 28, a bartender, is charged with retail theft for taking two pairs of wireless headphones worth $698 from an electronics store.

Security video shows a person in a gray baseball cap placing the headphones inside a backpack and leaving without paying at 4:12 p.m. The video is low resolution, and the face is hidden by the cap. Twenty minutes earlier, the same person bought a phone charger at the register and scanned a loyalty card registered to the defendant.

The backpack in the video has a red rectangular patch on the front pocket. Police seized a backpack from the defendant's apartment with a similar red patch, which the defendant says the defendant sewed on themself; patches of that style are sold widely online. At 9:30 p.m. that evening, the defendant's phone searched for the resale price of the exact headphone model. No headphones were found in the apartment.

The defendant testified that the defendant often lets friends use the defendant's loyalty card number for discounts, that friends sometimes borrow the backpack, and that the defendant looked up the price because the defendant was thinking of buying the same headphones.

The defendant, 40, a high school teacher, is charged with retail theft of merchandise worth over $500 from a department store.

A store detective saw the defendant remove the security tags from two winter coats in a fitting room and leave the store wearing one coat and carrying the other in a shopping bag. The defendant was stopped outside with both coats. The ticket price on each coat was $265, for a total of $530.

That weekend, a sign on the coat rack read "30% off all outerwear" in large letters and, in small print at the bottom, "for loyalty members, at the register." The defendant is not a loyalty member. At the member price, the total would have been $371. The store manager testified that non-members always pay the ticket price.

The defendant does not deny leaving with the coats. The defendant testified that the defendant meant to pay at a register on another floor and forgot because the defendant was on a phone call. The removed tags were found in the fitting room trash can.

The defendant, 23, a part-time grocery store clerk, is charged with retail theft of vitamins and electric toothbrushes worth $544 from a drugstore.

The defendant entered the store with an acquaintance. A camera shows the two walking together through the health products aisle, where the acquaintance's back blocks the view of the shelves for about 40 seconds. After the alarm sounded at the exit, a store employee found the merchandise in a tote bag carried by the defendant. The acquaintance ran away and was never charged.

The defendant testified that the defendant did not know the items were in the defendant's bag and that the acquaintance had asked to "put something" in it while the defendant was looking at the defendant's phone. A forensic report on the defendant's phone shows that the screen was locked during those 40 seconds. The defendant said the defendant may have been reading notifications on the lock screen. The employee testified that, when the alarm went off, the defendant said, "Please don't call the police."

The acquaintance has two prior shoplifting convictions and could not be found to testify.

The defendant, 35, a real estate agent, is charged with retail theft for taking four smart home cameras worth $760 from a big-box store.

Store video shows a person in a gray rain jacket and sunglasses taking the cameras from a shelf and leaving through the garden center exit without paying. The face is not clearly visible. Two days later, four cameras of the same model, still sealed, were listed for sale on an online marketplace. The listing account was created with the defendant's email address, and the listing photos were taken on a kitchen counter that matches the one in the defendant's apartment. The defendant admits owning a gray rain jacket.

Marketplace records show that the account was accessed from two phones, one of which belongs to the defendant. The other phone was never identified.

The defendant testified that a short-term guest renting a room in the defendant's apartment that week must have used the defendant's account to list the cameras. The defendant could not provide the guest's full name, and the booking was paid in cash.

The defendant, 46, a postal carrier, is charged with retail theft for leaving a warehouse club with a television worth $649 that had not been paid for.

The defendant went through a staffed checkout with a full cart. The cashier scanned 31 items worth $287, but the television, in a large box on the lower rack of the cart, was not scanned. At the exit, the receipt checker noticed the box and stopped the defendant.

The checkout line video shows that, about a minute before reaching the cashier, the defendant took a bulky pack of paper towels from the top of the cart and placed it on the lower rack, partly covering the television box. The cashier testified to asking, as usual, "anything on the bottom?" and believes the defendant answered "no," but admitted to asking that question dozens of times an hour. The video has no audio.

The defendant testified that the defendant moved the paper towels to make room for other items on top and that the defendant did not hear the question in the noisy checkout area. The defendant paid with a membership card in the defendant's own name.

The defendant, 30, a pharmacist, is charged with retail theft for taking three bottles of premium wine worth $540 from a supermarket.

A loss prevention officer testified to watching the defendant put the three bottles into a large shoulder bag in the wine aisle. The officer followed the defendant but lost sight of the defendant for about one minute when the defendant turned into a hallway leading to the restrooms and to a side door to the parking lot. The defendant then walked out through the main exit without paying for anything. The officer stopped the defendant in the parking lot and searched the bag, which contained no wine. Thirty minutes later, staff found the three bottles behind a planter just outside the side door.

The hallway camera shows the defendant entering and leaving the hallway; it also shows the side door opening once during that minute, but a stack of boxes blocks the view of who opened it.

The defendant testified that the defendant changed the defendant's mind about the wine and left the bottles on a shelf in the hallway, and that someone else must have carried them outside. The officer testified that there is no shelf in that hallway; the defendant then said the defendant may have set them on the stack of boxes.

The defendant, 27, a call center representative, is charged with retail theft for a return scheme at a sporting goods store. Prosecutors say the defendant took two pairs of hiking boots from the shelves, then "returned" them at the service desk using an old receipt, receiving $520 in store credit.

Video shows the defendant entering the store with a folded shopping bag, walking to the footwear section, and going to the service desk with two boxes of boots about ten minutes later. The footwear camera shows the defendant near the boot shelves but does not show the defendant removing boxes. The receipt the defendant used came from a purchase made three weeks earlier with a credit card that does not belong to the defendant.

The defendant testified that an acquaintance handed the defendant the receipt and the boots in the parking lot and promised to split the credit. The defendant said the defendant walked to the footwear section only to compare prices. Phone records show several calls between the defendant and an unregistered number that morning.

The defendant, 37, an assistant store manager, is charged with retail theft for removing two laptops worth $1,480 from the stockroom of the electronics store where the defendant worked.

The store's access system shows that the defendant's badge opened the stockroom at 9:52 p.m., after closing. Inventory counted the next morning was short two laptops. The stockroom camera was pointed at the loading dock and did not show the shelves. The rear door alarm was turned off with the manager code, which is known to four employees, including the defendant.

A sales associate testified that, that afternoon, the defendant asked whether the stockroom camera "still points at the dock." The defendant testified that the defendant asked because the defendant had suggested moving the camera weeks earlier.

The defendant testified that the defendant lost the defendant's badge two days before the theft and told the store manager in person. The store manager says the only report was a text message sent the morning after the theft. No laptops were found.

The defendant, 22, a university student, is charged with retail theft of sunglasses worth $585 from a boutique in a shopping mall.

A sales associate testified to seeing a customer in a green jacket slip four pairs of designer sunglasses into a coat pocket while the associate was helping another customer, and to seeing the customer's face clearly for a few seconds. The customer left with a group of four people. About five minutes later, mall security brought the associate to the food court, pointed out the group, and asked whether the person was there. The associate immediately pointed to the defendant, the only person in the group wearing a green jacket. The four pairs of sunglasses were found in a trash can about ten meters from the group's table.

The associate admitted that two other customers in the store that afternoon also wore green. The boutique camera was not recording because of a system update. No sunglasses were found on the defendant or on any other member of the group.

The defendant testified that the defendant was in the boutique only briefly and never touched the sunglasses.

The defendant, 32, an insurance appraiser, is charged with residential burglary of a detached house. While the owners were away for a weekend, someone forced open a rear window and took jewelry, a laptop, and about $800 in cash.

Investigators lifted two fingerprints from the inside surface of the forced window frame, the side facing the room. Both matched the defendant. Fresh pry marks on the outside of the frame matched a flat screwdriver, a common tool. About five weeks earlier, the defendant had inspected storm damage to the rear windows for the owners' insurance company. The inspection report, signed by the defendant, describes an "exterior inspection only."

The owners testified that they did not let anyone into the house during the inspection and did not see the inspector open any window. A fingerprint expert testified that prints on a painted frame can last for weeks and that their age cannot be determined.

The defendant testified that the defendant opened the window from outside to check the seal, which would have meant touching the inner surface, and that the defendant did not record it because it was routine. The defendant's roommate confirmed that the defendant was home Saturday evening but away Sunday afternoon, when the neighbors believe the burglary happened.

The defendant, 29, a restaurant shift manager, is charged with residential burglary of an apartment from which a gold watch, two rings, and a tablet were taken between 1:00 p.m. and 4:00 p.m.

Two days after the burglary, the defendant sold the gold watch to a pawn shop, showing the defendant's own driver's license and signing the receipt. The watch had a unique engraving that the owner described before it was recovered. Its market value is about $1,200. The other items were never found.

The defendant testified that the defendant bought the watch for $150 from a stranger at a gas station and sold it to the pawn shop for $400 the same week. The defendant could not give the stranger's name or a clear description. The gas station's cameras keep footage for only 24 hours.

There were no fingerprints, shoe prints, or DNA linking the defendant to the apartment. Phone company records show that the defendant's phone was switched off from 12:40 p.m. to 4:25 p.m. that day, the only time it was off that month. The defendant said the battery died. The defendant lives about 15 minutes from the apartment.

The defendant, 25, a junior accountant, is charged with residential burglary of a townhouse. Someone kicked in the back door on a weekday morning and took two laptops and a gaming console. The owners were at work from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. that day.

Investigators photographed a muddy shoe print on the kitchen floor. The print matches the sole pattern and size of a running shoe found in the defendant's closet. A shoe expert testified that the model is one of the best-selling running shoes in the country.

Cell tower data place the defendant's phone in the area of the townhouse between 9:00 and 11:30 a.m. The defendant's friend lives about four blocks away and testified that the defendant came over that morning to help move furniture, but left "for a while" at some point; the friend could not say when or for how long. None of the stolen items were found.

The defendant, 38, a sales representative, is charged with residential burglary of a house. Someone broke a glass panel in the back door and stole a coin collection worth about $9,000.

A cigarette butt found on the back patio, about two meters from the broken door, contained the defendant's DNA. The defendant lived in the house next door until three months before the burglary and sometimes smoked on the homeowners' patio during backyard gatherings. A lab analyst testified that the DNA showed little degradation, "more consistent with days than with months" outdoors, but that the age of a sample cannot be determined with certainty. It had rained twice in the week before the burglary.

The homeowners had shown the coin collection to several visitors over the years, including the defendant. A neighbor's camera recorded a car similar to the defendant's, a common silver sedan, passing on the street 40 minutes before the estimated time of the burglary. The plate is not readable.

The defendant testified that the defendant was at the defendant's new apartment that evening. The defendant has no witnesses. Bank records show that the defendant had fallen behind on rent and had received an eviction warning the week before.

The defendant, 27, a graphic designer, is charged with residential burglary of an apartment the defendant used to share with the complainant. Three months after the defendant moved out, someone entered the apartment while it was empty and took a camera, two lenses, and an envelope with $1,500 in cash.

There was no forced entry. The defendant admits never returning the defendant's key. The complainant testified that two other people also had keys: a dog walker and a former partner of the complainant. Both testified that they did not enter the apartment that day.

The complainant testified that the defendant knew where the cash envelope was kept. A text message from the defendant, sent two weeks before the burglary, says: "You still owe me for the last two months of utilities, and I'm going to get it one way or another." Two days after the burglary, the defendant deposited $1,400 in cash into the defendant's bank account.

The defendant testified that the message was about filing a small claims case and that the cash came from selling furniture to buyers the defendant found online; the defendant produced one listing for a sofa priced at $300. The defendant says the defendant was working alone at home that afternoon.

The defendant, 34, a hospital pharmacist who works night shifts, is charged with residential burglary after being found at about 3:30 a.m. inside the attached garage of a house two blocks from the defendant's own home. Under state law, an attached garage is part of the dwelling.

The homeowner heard noises, looked out, and saw a person with a flashlight working at the side door of the garage for about a minute before stepping inside. The homeowner called 911. Police arrived within six minutes and found the defendant inside the garage, wearing gloves and holding a flashlight, next to a shelf with power tools. Nothing was missing.

The defendant testified that the defendant's cat had escaped that evening and that the defendant was searching nearby yards. The defendant said the defendant heard a noise inside the garage, found the side door unlocked, and stepped in to look for the cat. A "lost cat" post from the defendant appeared on a local community app at 1:50 a.m. The cat was found two days later, three streets away.

The homeowner testified that the side door was locked earlier that night. Officers photographed fresh-looking scratches around the latch; a detective said they were consistent with a thin tool. No tool was found on the defendant, and no older photos of the door exist for comparison.

The defendant, 26, a barista, is charged with residential burglary of a house from which a laptop, a tablet, and a set of headphones were stolen during the day.

The laptop had tracking software. Two days after the burglary, the owner located it at a house where the defendant rents a room with three other tenants. Police found the laptop in a shared living room. Its browser history shows the defendant's personal email account being opened on it the day after the burglary. The tablet and headphones were not found.

One of the other tenants had moved out the day after the burglary and could not be located. The defendant testified that this tenant brought the laptop home, said it had been "bought cheap from a friend," and let the defendant use it once to check email. The remaining two tenants testified that they had never seen the laptop but rarely used the living room.

A neighbor of the burglarized house saw a person on a bicycle leave the house carrying a backpack. The defendant owns a bicycle, as do the other tenants. Phone location data place the defendant at work during most of the estimated burglary window, but there is a 50-minute gap during the defendant's lunch break; the house is about 10 minutes away by bicycle.

The defendant, 31, a postal mail carrier, is charged with residential burglary of a house on the defendant's delivery route. Someone entered through an unlocked back door during the day and took a tablet, a laptop, and several pieces of jewelry.

A neighbor testified to seeing the defendant, whom the neighbor recognized as the regular mail carrier, walking along the side of the house toward the backyard at about 2:00 p.m. Postal scan records show that the defendant delivered a package to that house at 1:57 p.m., leaving it at the front door. The postal vehicle's GPS shows the defendant at the next stop four minutes later.

The GPS also shows that, at 4:40 p.m., after the defendant's route had ended, the postal vehicle returned to the same street and stayed parked two houses away for 12 minutes. The homeowners left for work at 8:00 a.m. and returned at 6:30 p.m. A different neighbor saw a person in a gray sweatshirt in the backyard "sometime in the afternoon" but could not describe the face.

The defendant testified that the defendant walked toward the side gate at 2:00 p.m. only to look for a safer place to leave the package, and that the defendant returned at 4:40 p.m. to eat a late lunch in a shaded spot the defendant often uses.

The defendant, 36, a freelance photographer, is charged with residential burglary of a house where a glass patio door was smashed and electronics worth about $4,000 were taken.

Police stopped the defendant about one kilometer from the house, 50 minutes after a neighbor reported the sound of breaking glass. A lab found three tiny glass fragments on the defendant's jacket with the same refractive index as the patio door glass, a type used in millions of doors. Blue fibers on the broken door frame were consistent with the defendant's jacket, a mass-produced item.

The defendant testified that the defendant spent the evening at a friend's home helping repair a broken window, which explains the glass. The friend confirmed this and showed a receipt for window glass bought that afternoon, but an expert testified that the friend's window used a different type of glass. No stolen items were found on the defendant or in the defendant's car. The defendant has a conviction for burglary from 11 years ago.

The defendant, 41, an insurance broker, is charged with residential burglary of a house from which a safe containing about $20,000 in cash and documents was removed. The owners were away for the weekend when it happened.

A person who shared a jail cell with the defendant for three days, after the defendant's arrest on an unrelated traffic warrant, testified that the defendant described "taking a safe out of a house on the lake road" and said it took two people to carry it. In exchange for testifying, the informant received a reduced sentence on a fraud charge. Those details had appeared in a local news article.

Investigators found that the defendant paid off a $6,000 car loan in cash two weeks after the burglary. The defendant testified that the money came from selling a boat and produced a handwritten bill of sale; the buyer could not be located. The defendant denies ever talking about the burglary.

The defendant, 39, a staff accountant, is charged with embezzlement from the furniture company where the defendant worked. Over seven months, 14 payments totaling $48,300 were sent from the company's bank account to a vendor that does not exist. The vendor's bank account was opened online with a stolen identity.

All 14 payments were approved in the accounting system under the defendant's login. The defendant was one of three people in the accounting office, and the office shared one computer for bank approvals. Two coworkers testified that the defendant's password was written on a sticky note attached to that computer's monitor.

Four of the payments were approved on days when the defendant was working from home; the remote access logs show the defendant's account connected from the defendant's home internet address on those days. No payments were made during the two weeks the defendant was on vacation, although the other two employees worked as usual.

The defendant testified that the defendant never approved those payments and that anyone in the office could have used the defendant's login, even remotely, once they knew the password. Investigators found no unusual deposits in the defendant's bank accounts. The defendant had taken on a large personal loan the year before.

The defendant, 44, an office operations manager, is charged with embezzlement from a small architecture firm. Over two years, the defendant deposited 22 company checks, totaling $36,750, into the defendant's personal bank account. The firm has eight employees and an outside accountant who reviews the books once a year.

The defendant admits making the deposits. The defendant testified that one of the firm's two founding partners verbally authorized the checks as reimbursement for expenses the defendant paid personally and as an informal bonus. That partner died suddenly. The surviving partner testified to knowing nothing about any such agreement, and the firm's written policy requires receipts for every reimbursement.

The defendant produced receipts for about $9,400 in business expenses. Two of the checks bear the deceased partner's signature; the others were signed with a signature stamp that the defendant was allowed to use for routine bills.

The firm's bookkeeper testified that the deceased partner "was informal about money" and sometimes gave bonuses without recording them.

The defendant, 26, a shift supervisor at a gas station convenience store, is charged with embezzlement of about $6,200 in cash over three months.

The store's records show cash shortages on 13 shifts. The defendant supervised 9 of them, and those 9 shortages averaged $620. The 4 shortages on shifts the defendant did not work averaged $150. On the defendant's shifts, two cashiers also had access to the registers, but the supervisor was the only person with the code to the safe where cash was dropped.

The camera above the safe shows the defendant opening the safe 38 times during those shifts. The video shows the defendant counting cash, but the angle does not show whether any was removed. After the defendant was suspended, shortages stopped for six weeks and then occurred twice more, for $90 and $120.

A cashier testified to once seeing the defendant put "a folded stack of bills" into a jacket pocket; the defendant testified that it was the defendant's own tip money from a second job. The defendant's bank records show cash deposits of $100 to $200 most weeks during the period, which the defendant says came from weekend work for a wedding photographer; the defendant produced two payment messages from the photographer.

The defendant, 35, an accounting systems analyst responsible for payroll processing, is charged with embezzlement from a regional trucking company. For 15 months, a person who never worked at the company received biweekly paychecks totaling $41,600, deposited into an account controlled by the company's operations manager.

The defendant created the fake employee record and approved each pay run. The defendant admits creating the record but testified that the operations manager said the person was a remote dispatcher hired off the books and told the defendant to "just put them in the system." Company policy required payroll staff to verify every new employee with a signed hiring form. No form exists.

An email from the defendant to the operations manager, sent a week after the record was created, says: "Make sure the new dispatcher doesn't end up on the org chart." The defendant testified that the defendant wrote it because the manager had said the hire was confidential.

The operations manager was also charged and agreed to testify against the defendant in exchange for a reduced sentence. The manager testified that the defendant came up with the scheme and received $500 in cash from each paycheck. The defendant bought a used car with $7,000 in cash during the period; the defendant testified that the money came from savings.

The defendant, 24, a customer service desk associate at a department store, is charged with embezzlement for processing refunds onto the defendant's own debit card. Over four months, 31 refunds totaling $5,860 were paid to a card in the defendant's name.

The defendant admits that the refunds went to the defendant's card. The defendant testified that some customers who had paid in cash wanted their refunds immediately, so the defendant refunded those amounts to the defendant's own card and handed the customers cash from the defendant's wallet, because the store's cash refund process took too long. The defendant said a former supervisor told the defendant this was acceptable; the former supervisor denies it.

The store found returned merchandise logged for 6 of the 31 refunds. For the other 25, there is no record of returned items. Store video for three of those refunds shows no customer at the desk. The refunds stopped the day after managers announced an audit of the service desk.

The defendant withdrew cash from ATMs on most of the days the refunds were processed, which the defense says is consistent with replacing the cash the defendant gave to customers.

The defendant, 31, an inventory analyst at an electronics distributor, is charged with embezzlement of company inventory. Over six months, 46 new graphics cards worth $27,000 disappeared from the warehouse, and inventory records were adjusted to hide the losses.

The adjustments were made under the defendant's user account, which the defendant admits only the defendant uses. An online seller account, shipping from the defendant's home address, sold 39 graphics cards of the same model during that period. The seller account was registered to the defendant's housemate, a forklift operator at the same warehouse. The housemate invoked the right to remain silent.

The defendant testified that the defendant made the adjustments because physical counts were lower than system counts, which was the defendant's job, and that the defendant reported the losses. The warehouse manager confirms two emails from the defendant about shortages, but says the defendant described them as counting errors.

Payments from the seller account went to the housemate's bank account. During the six months, the housemate transferred $6,000 to the defendant. The defendant's share of the rent is $650 per month, or $3,900 for the period. The defendant says the rest covered shared bills and repaid a personal loan the defendant had made to the housemate, which was never written down.

The defendant, 47, a regional sales director at a medical equipment company, is charged with embezzlement for using a corporate credit card for personal purchases. An internal audit found $23,900 in charges over one year that the company classified as personal: weekend hotel stays, restaurant meals near the defendant's home, and electronics.

The defendant testified that most of the charges were legitimate client entertainment and travel and that the defendant lost a folder of receipts during a move. The defendant's former manager testified that the receipt policy was "loosely enforced" for senior sales staff. Two clients testified that the defendant took them to dinner several times near the defendant's home but could not remember the dates.

The audit found that 11 weekend hotel stays were in a resort town where the defendant has no clients; a conference was held there on only two of those weekends. The electronics, a laptop and two tablets, were not in the company's asset records; the defendant testified that the defendant used them for client presentations.

The defendant, 30, an operations coordinator at a nonprofit food bank, is charged with embezzlement of $18,400 in donations. Donations made through a campaign page that the defendant managed were sent to a payment account opened in the defendant's name instead of the nonprofit's account.

The defendant testified that the defendant never opened the payment account and that the defendant's identity had been stolen. The defendant had filed a police report about identity theft four months earlier, after someone opened a credit card in the defendant's name.

The campaign page's logs show that the defendant's staff login changed the page's payout destination to the new account on the same day that account was opened. The food bank's director testified that the defendant was the only staff member who changed the page settings during the period. The defendant said the defendant did not remember making that change and that the defendant's login could have been stolen too.

Of the money, $6,000 paid off the defendant's overdue car loan and $3,200 went to the defendant's landlord. The defendant testified that the defendant did not notice those payments because the defendant had set up automatic payments from several accounts. The rest was withdrawn in cash at ATMs in another city.

The defendant, 37, a treasury analyst at a community credit union, is charged with embezzlement of $52,000. Over two years, small amounts were moved from dormant member accounts into an internal suspense account and then transferred to an outside account belonging to a company registered under a false name.

A spreadsheet tracking the dormant accounts and each transfer was found on the defendant's work computer. The transfers were made with two employee logins: the defendant's and that of a coworker who left the credit union a year earlier and could not be found.

After a three-hour meeting with the board and the credit union's lawyer, the defendant wrote an email to the board: "I should have reported what was happening with the dormant accounts. I'm sorry for my part in this." The defendant testified that the defendant's "part" was failing to report transfers the defendant had noticed and that the spreadsheet was the defendant's own effort to track the problem.

The outside company's bank account was opened with a phone number that once belonged to the former coworker.

The defendant, 43, a facilities coordinator at a commercial property company, is charged with embezzlement for selling the company's surplus office furniture and keeping the money. Over 18 months, the defendant sold surplus furniture from building renovations to a used furniture dealer 17 times, receiving $14,700.

The defendant admits the sales. The defendant testified that a former facilities director told the defendant years earlier that staff could "take care of the old furniture" and keep the proceeds, and that this had long been the practice. A maintenance technician who worked at the company for 12 years testified that the previous coordinator also sold surplus furniture and kept the money. The former director could not be located.

Each year, the defendant signed an asset policy acknowledgment stating that "surplus furniture and equipment remain company property until disposed of through the facilities office." The defendant testified that the defendant signed it with other routine forms without reading it closely. The defendant did not report the income on the defendant's tax returns and never mentioned the sales to the current director, who joined two years ago.

The defendant, 29, a pharmacy manager, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a cyclist at about 11:20 p.m. on a two-lane road. The cyclist suffered a broken leg. A witness wrote down a partial plate and described a silver hatchback.

Police found the defendant's silver hatchback the next morning with a cracked headlight and a dent on the front right fender. Paint transfer from the bicycle matched the dent, and the plate matches the partial plate.

The defendant shares the car with the defendant's housemate, and both have keys. The defendant testified that the defendant was asleep at home that night and that the housemate had borrowed the car. The housemate testified to returning the car at 9:30 p.m. and staying home afterward.

At 11:05 p.m., the defendant's credit card paid for fuel at a gas station three kilometers from the collision. The station's camera was not working. The defendant testified that the housemate sometimes uses the card for gas with the defendant's permission; the housemate denies using it that night.

The witness saw the driver only from behind and could not describe the person. The car's seat position fit both people.

The defendant, 52, a high school chemistry teacher, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a pedestrian at about 6:40 p.m. on a rainy winter evening. The pedestrian was walking at the edge of a narrow street without sidewalks, was struck by a side mirror, and fell into a ditch, suffering a broken wrist and a concussion.

The defendant admits driving on that street at the time and admits feeling "a bump." The defendant testified that the defendant thought the defendant had hit a pothole, which is common on that street, and kept driving home. The next morning, the defendant reported the broken right side mirror to the defendant's insurer as pothole damage.

A neighbor who heard the impact testified that it was "a loud bang" and that the car did not slow down. It was raining hard, and the defendant said the radio was on.

An accident reconstruction expert testified that a driver could have seen the pedestrian in the headlights for about two seconds before impact, but that after impact the pedestrian fell to the right, outside the driver's line of sight. The pedestrian was wearing dark clothing.

The defendant, 34, a software tester, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a motorcyclist at an intersection at about 1:15 a.m. A traffic camera recorded a gray SUV running a red light, hitting the motorcycle, and driving away. The image shows the plate, registered to the defendant, but not the driver.

At 7:40 a.m. the same morning, the defendant reported the SUV stolen from the street outside the defendant's apartment. Police found the SUV two days later, abandoned in a parking lot about three kilometers from the collision, with front-end damage. The ignition had been forced with a tool. A detective testified that thieves usually force ignitions, but that owners covering up a crime sometimes damage their own cars.

Router records show that the defendant's phone disconnected from the defendant's home Wi-Fi at 12:40 a.m. and reconnected at 1:50 a.m. The defendant testified that the defendant was asleep and that the phone sometimes drops the connection overnight; the records show no other disconnection that week. The defendant's apartment is about 15 minutes from the intersection.

The defendant has a prior conviction for driving under the influence from five years ago, which the prosecution offers as a motive to avoid another arrest.

The defendant, 27, a restaurant host, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a pedestrian in a crosswalk at about 9:50 p.m. The pedestrian suffered a fractured hip.

A bus driver waiting at the light testified to seeing the driver's face through the side window for "a second or two" as the car turned and drove off. The street lighting was poor. Days later, the bus driver saw the defendant in the courtroom during a preliminary hearing, where the defendant was the only person charged, and said, "That's the driver." The bus driver was never shown a photo lineup.

The defendant's blue sedan has a dent in the front bumper. A paint expert testified that the dent is consistent with hitting a person but could also have come from a low-speed impact with a pole. The defendant testified that the defendant hit a parking pole a week earlier.

Phone location data place the defendant's phone about 600 meters before the crosswalk at 9:44 p.m. and about 400 meters past it, on the same road, at 9:53 p.m. The defendant testified that the defendant turned off before the crosswalk and took a side street; an analyst testified that the location points are accurate only to about 300 meters.

The defendant, 38, a hotel operations manager, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured another driver at about 5:30 p.m. in a supermarket parking lot exit.

The other driver testified that the defendant's car backed into the driver's door. The defendant got out, looked at the damage, said something like "it's just a scratch," and drove away before the two exchanged information. The other driver later went to an emergency clinic with neck pain and was diagnosed with a whiplash injury.

Data from the defendant's car's event recorder show an impact at 5:31 p.m. at 9 km/h. The supermarket camera shows the defendant standing next to the other car for about 70 seconds, then leaving. During that time, the other driver stays seated and, at least twice, holds a hand to the back of the neck. The video has no audio.

The defendant testified that the other driver said "don't worry about it" and waved the defendant off, and that the defendant did not notice any sign of injury. The other driver denies saying that. The defendant called the supermarket the next day to ask whether anyone had reported damage.

The defendant, 33, a sales account manager, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a jogger on a rural road at about 6:15 a.m. The jogger suffered a broken arm and could not describe the car.

Investigators recovered pieces of a headlight lens at the scene. The pieces match the headlight design of a popular compact car model, one of the best-selling cars in the state; the defendant owns that model.

The next morning, the defendant took the car to a small repair shop and paid $420 in cash to replace a headlight and repair a front fender. The shop owner testified that the fender damage "looked a few weeks old" because of rust spots, but admitted to not being an expert. The old headlight was thrown away before police could examine it.

The defendant testified that the defendant had hit a deer two weeks earlier and finally had time to fix the car. The defendant had not reported the deer collision. Phone company records show that the defendant's phone left the defendant's home at 6:05 a.m.; the defendant's usual commute passes the rural road about ten minutes later. The defendant said the defendant took a different route that day but could not name any stop along it.

The defendant, 41, a real estate appraiser, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a motorcyclist on a highway at about 3:00 p.m. The motorcyclist suffered a fractured collarbone.

A dashcam in another car recorded the defendant's SUV changing lanes and clipping the front wheel of a motorcycle that was in the SUV's blind spot. The motorcyclist fell and slid onto the shoulder. The SUV continued at the same speed and left at the next exit. The defendant admits that the defendant was driving.

The defendant testified that the defendant checked the defendant's mirrors, did not see the motorcycle, and did not feel any impact. An expert for the prosecution testified that the contact would have caused "a noticeable jolt." An expert for the defense testified that a light contact with the rear corner of a heavy SUV may not be felt.

The SUV had a scuff mark on the rear bumper. The defendant learned about the collision when police came to the defendant's home two days later.

The defendant, 36, a museum educator, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a pedestrian at about 12:40 a.m. The pedestrian suffered a broken pelvis.

A security camera recorded a dark gray sedan with a car-sharing company logo hitting the pedestrian and driving away. Company records show that the sedan was unlocked with the defendant's membership account at 11:52 p.m. and returned two kilometers away at 1:05 a.m. The sedan was later found with front-end damage.

The defendant testified that, that night, the defendant had lent the defendant's account login to an acquaintance whose own membership was suspended. The car was unlocked through the app from a phone that was not the defendant's usual device; police never identified that phone. The acquaintance named by the defendant denies borrowing the account.

The defendant's phone stayed at a friend's party across town from 10:00 p.m. to 2:00 a.m. Two guests testified that the defendant was at the party early on but left "around midnight, maybe a bit before"; one said the defendant had left the phone charging in the kitchen. The party is about 10 minutes by car from where the sedan was unlocked.

The defendant, 25, a graduate student, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a pedestrian outside a concert venue at about 11:55 p.m. The pedestrian suffered a head injury.

Several people saw the defendant's car pull out of a parking spot quickly and saw the pedestrian fall in the street next to the car. Two witnesses said they saw the car's bumper hit the pedestrian. A third said the pedestrian stepped off the curb, tripped, and fell next to the car without being hit. The pedestrian, who had also been drinking, remembers nothing.

The venue's camera shows the car's brake lights coming on as the pedestrian falls, the car stopping for about two seconds, and then accelerating away. The angle does not show whether the bumper touched the pedestrian. A forensic examination found no damage, fibers, or biological traces on the defendant's car. The emergency physician testified that the injury is consistent with a fall from standing height, with or without being struck.

A breath test three hours later showed a blood alcohol level of 0.05; an expert estimated about 0.09 at the time. The defendant testified that the defendant saw someone fall near the car, thought the person had tripped, and left because the defendant was afraid of being caught driving after drinking.

The defendant, 31, a city planner, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a teenager riding an electric scooter at about 8:20 p.m. The rider suffered a broken ankle and remembers only a "gray car."

Phone location data place the defendant's phone on the same street at 8:19 p.m. The defendant drives a gray compact car. At about 9:20 p.m., the defendant's phone searched for "what happens if you hit someone and drive away" and "how long do police keep traffic camera footage." The nearest traffic camera was not working that night.

Investigators found no damage on the defendant's car. A mechanic testified that a scooter could hit a car without leaving visible damage. The rider's scooter had a scrape of gray paint, too small to compare. At least 40 gray compact cars are registered within two kilometers of the scene.

The defendant testified that the defendant was driving home on that street but did not hit anyone, and that the searches were prompted by a true-crime podcast about a hit-and-run case. The defendant's podcast app shows that episode starting at 9:40 p.m., after the searches. The defendant said the defendant had heard an earlier episode of the same series that afternoon; the app shows no other episode played that day.
